## Overview

A rule says how a cell changes given its neighbours; the **space** says where
the cells are and what lies beyond an edge, and the **neighbourhood** says
which cells count as neighbours. Both are independent of the rule, so the same
rule can run on a torus, a bounded grid, a hexagonal grid, a three-dimensional
lattice or an arbitrary graph.

| space | constructor | cells |
|---|---|---|
| periodic square lattice, any dimension | `Torus(dims...)` | `CartesianIndex` |
| square lattice with edges | `Grid(dims...; boundary)` | `CartesianIndex` |
| hexagonal lattice | `HexGrid(nq, nr; boundary)` | `CartesianIndex` (axial) |
| irregular network | `GraphSpace(n, edges)` | `Int` |

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Random
```

## Edges

Each axis of a lattice has a boundary condition:

- `Periodic()`: the axis wraps around.
- `Constant(v)`: every cell beyond the edge holds `v`.
- `Reflecting()`: the axis is mirrored at the edge, with the edge cell repeated.

`Torus(dims...)` is periodic on every axis; `Grid(dims...; boundary)` takes one
boundary for all axes or a tuple with one per axis. Here a glider heading
down and to the right meets the edge of a 16 × 16 board under four boundary
conditions:

```{julia}
glider, _ = parse_rle(raw"""
x = 3, y = 3
bo$2bo$3o!
""")
u0 = place!(zeros(Int8, 16, 16), glider, (6, 6))
spaces = ["torus" => Torus(16, 16),
          "dead edges" => Grid(16, 16; boundary=Constant(0)),
          "reflecting" => Grid(16, 16; boundary=Reflecting()),
          "cylinder" => Grid(16, 16; boundary=(Periodic(), Constant(0)))]
panels = map(spaces) do (name, space)
    plot(solve(CAProblem(Life(), u0, 40; space)); c=:binary, colorbar=false,
         title=name, titlefontsize=10)
end
plot(panels...; layout=(1, 4), size=(900, 250))
```

On the torus the glider leaves at the bottom right and re-enters at the top
left, unharmed. Against dead edges it collides with the corner and settles
into a block. The reflecting edge also turns it into a block, a little away
from the corner, because the mirrored cells beyond the edge interact with it.
The cylinder wraps vertically but not horizontally, so the glider meets the
right-hand edge and becomes a block straddling the top and bottom rows.

A `Constant` edge need not be empty. Rule 30 on a line whose margins are live:

```{julia}
space = Grid(80; boundary=Constant(1))
plot(solve(CAProblem(Wolfram(30), zeros(Int8, 80), 60; space));
     c=:binary, colorbar=false, size=(600, 350), title="Rule 30 with live edges")
```

## Neighbourhoods

Every built-in neighbourhood is turned into explicit offsets from the centre
cell. The centre itself is never a neighbour; a rule receives it separately.
Offsets are listed with the first axis varying fastest:

```{julia}
neighbourhood_offsets(VonNeumann(1), Torus(5, 5))
```

The neighbour states a rule receives are in exactly this order. To see the
shapes, mark the offsets on a small board:

```{julia}
function show_neighbourhood(nb, space=Torus(11, 11); title=string(nb))
    m = zeros(Int, size(space))
    c = CartesianIndex(6, 6)
    for o in neighbourhood_offsets(nb, space).offsets
        m[c + o] = 1
    end
    m[c] = 2
    return plot(space, m; c=[:white, :steelblue, :black], colorbar=false, title,
                titlefontsize=10, ticks=false)
end
knight = Offsets((1, 2), (2, 1), (2, -1), (1, -2), (-1, -2), (-2, -1), (-2, 1), (-1, 2))
plot(show_neighbourhood(Moore(1)), show_neighbourhood(Moore(2)),
     show_neighbourhood(VonNeumann(2)), show_neighbourhood(knight; title="knight's moves");
     layout=(1, 4), size=(900, 250))
```

`Life` and `Generations` use the space's default neighbourhood unless given
one. The same soup under two Life-like rules with unusual neighbourhoods:

```{julia}
soup = Int8.(rand(Xoshiro(1), 0:1, 80, 80))
plot(plot(solve(CAProblem(Life("B2/S2"; neighbourhood=VonNeumann(1)), soup, 60));
          c=:binary, colorbar=false, title="B2/S2, von Neumann"),
     plot(solve(CAProblem(Life("B3/S23"; neighbourhood=knight), soup, 60));
          c=:binary, colorbar=false, title="B3/S23, knight's moves");
     layout=(1, 2), size=(700, 350))
```

### Larger than Life

Radius-$r$ Moore neighbourhoods give the "Larger than Life" rules, whose
neighbour counts go well beyond 8. Counts are then given as ranges. Bosco's
rule is usually written `R5,C0,M1,S33..57,B34..45`, where `M1` means the centre
is included in the count. Counting neighbours only, as `Life` does, a live cell
survives with 32 to 56 live neighbours and a dead one is born with 34 to 45:

```{julia}
bosco = Life(34:45, 32:56; neighbourhood=Moore(5))
```

```{julia}
soup = Int8.(rand(Xoshiro(3), 0:1, 160, 160))
sol = solve(CAProblem(bosco, soup, 150); saveat=50)
plot([plot(sol; snapshot=i, c=:binary, colorbar=false) for i in 1:4]...; layout=(1, 4),
     size=(900, 250))
```

## Hexagonal grids

`HexGrid(nq, nr)` stores hexagonal cells in **axial coordinates**: cell
`(q, r)` sits at index `[q, r]`, and its six nearest neighbours are the cells
at offsets `(±1, 0)`, `(0, ±1)`, `(1, -1)` and `(-1, 1)`. The default
neighbourhood is `Hexagonal(1)`; `Hexagonal(2)` adds the second ring.

```{julia}
function show_hex_neighbourhood(r)
    space = HexGrid(9, 9)
    m = zeros(Int, 9, 9)
    c = CartesianIndex(5, 5)
    for o in neighbourhood_offsets(Hexagonal(r), space).offsets
        m[c + o] = 1
    end
    m[c] = 2
    return plot(space, m; c=[:white, :steelblue, :black], title="Hexagonal($r)",
                titlefontsize=10)
end
plot(show_hex_neighbourhood(1), show_hex_neighbourhood(2); layout=(1, 2), size=(700, 300))
```

The grid is drawn as a parallelogram because axial coordinates shear it; it is
periodic by default, so it tiles the plane. Life-like rules work unchanged,
counting six neighbours:

```{julia}
soup = Int8.(rand(Xoshiro(4), 0:1, 40, 40) .* (rand(Xoshiro(5), 40, 40) .< 0.4))
sol = solve(CAProblem(Life("B2/S34"), soup, 30; space=HexGrid(40, 40)))
plot(sol; c=[:white, :darkgreen], size=(700, 450), title="B2/S34 on a hexagonal grid")
```

## Three dimensions

Lattices can have any number of dimensions. Carter Bays' three-dimensional
Life rule "4555" is `B5/S45` with the 26-cell Moore neighbourhood:

```{julia}
soup3d = Int8.(rand(Xoshiro(6), 0:1, 32, 32, 32) .* (rand(Xoshiro(7), 32, 32, 32) .< 0.3))
sol = solve(CAProblem(Life("B5/S45"), soup3d, 40))
alive = [count(==(1), u) for u in sol.u]
plot(plot(sol.t, alive; xlabel="t", ylabel="live cells", legend=false),
     plot(Torus(32, 32), final_state(sol)[:, :, 16]; c=:binary, colorbar=false,
          title="slice z = 16 at t = 40");
     layout=(1, 2), size=(800, 330))
```

## Graphs

A `GraphSpace` is an arbitrary network: cell `i` reads the cells listed as its
neighbours, in order. It is built from a list of neighbour lists or from an
edge list (undirected unless `directed=true`). Rules see the neighbour states
as a vector, so the same code works for any degree.

As an example, a "complex contagion": a node adopts a behaviour (state `1`)
once at least half of its neighbours have, and never abandons it. On a ring
lattice where each node is linked to its four nearest neighbours, a few
adjacent adopters can start a cascade around the ring. Rewiring a fraction `p`
of the links at random (a Watts–Strogatz small world) shortens paths but
breaks up the local clusters that such a contagion relies on.

```{julia}
function small_world(n, k, p, rng)
    edges = Set{Tuple{Int,Int}}()
    for i in 1:n, j in 1:(k ÷ 2)
        a, b = i, mod1(i + j, n)
        if rand(rng) < p
            b = rand(rng, 1:n)
            while b == a || (min(a, b), max(a, b)) in edges
                b = rand(rng, 1:n)
            end
        end
        push!(edges, (min(a, b), max(a, b)))
    end
    return GraphSpace(n, collect(edges))
end

contagion = LocalRule() do cell, nbrs, ctx
    (cell == 1 || isempty(nbrs)) && return cell
    return count(==(1), nbrs) >= ctx.p.θ * length(nbrs) ? one(cell) : cell
end

n = 400
seeds = zeros(Int8, n)
seeds[1:4] .= 1
plt = plot(; xlabel="t", ylabel="fraction adopted", legend=:right)
for p in (0.0, 0.02, 0.1, 0.5)
    space = small_world(n, 4, p, Xoshiro(10))
    sol = solve(CAProblem(contagion, seeds, 150, (θ=0.5,); space))
    plot!(plt, sol.t, [sum(u) / n for u in sol.u]; label="p = $p")
end
plt
```

With no rewiring the cascade advances steadily around the ring, one node in
each direction per step. With even 2% of the links rewired it stops within a
few steps: a node whose link into the adopting cluster was moved elsewhere no
longer sees half of its neighbours adopting, and the front stalls there.
Shortcuts that would speed up a simple contagion block a complex one.
